lead.headline: Iran Says Indian Ships Can Cross the Strait of Hormuz
lead.deck: The narrow sea lane carries oil that India relies on, but ships there are still being hit and the US blockade is still in place.
body: Picture a narrow sea lane between Iran and Oman that carries oil India depends on. That is the Strait of Hormuz. This week an Iranian lawmaker, Amir Hayat Moqaddam, said vessels from India, China, Iraq and Qatar are allowed to cross it. Iran has effectively kept the strait shut since early in a war that began on 28 February.

Here is what India has at stake. The data firm Kpler counted 10.23 million barrels a day of Gulf crude moving through the strait in October. India received 13 percent of that oil, and China about 42 percent. Moqaddam said Indian and Chinese ships would pay Tehran a fee to cross, while Qatari ships would not.

Permission from Iran does not settle everything. The US says its naval blockade covers every vessel entering or leaving Iranian ports, and nobody has said whether Washington accepts the exemptions. More than 120 commercial ships have been hit in the region since the war began, and October was the worst month.

Talks are running alongside the danger. Qatar's prime minister urged the US and Iran not to wait for a 'perfect moment' to make a deal, and President Trump said 'we've made a lot of progress' without giving details. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he spoke with 12 foreign ministers in 48 hours. An analyst at IG Group said the exemptions change little for oil markets for now.

lead.why: Oil moves fuel and shipping prices, so a sea lane far away can reach family budgets in India and the United States. Iran's exemption helps only if ships are safe, and the strait is still dangerous.

world.headline: Octopuses Squeeze Through Tight Holes One Arm at a Time
world.deck: A study filmed seven octopuses fitting through holes in boxes and found a step-by-step method.
body: An octopus is soft, but it does have a rigid part: cartilage around its brain. Researchers wanted to see how that part affects the holes an octopus can fit through. They measured the distance between each octopus's eyes as a stand-in for the size of its most rigid cartilage.

The team tested three common octopuses and four Mayan octopuses. They gave each animal acrylic boxes with holes slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. The study appeared in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

For the wider holes, the octopuses followed three steps in a few seconds. First they pushed one or two arms through. Then they threaded a couple more through. Last, they used the arms already outside to pull the head and the remaining arms after them.
The narrower holes needed four steps. Common octopuses first pushed all their arms through, then squeezed the head and the bulbous mantle through.

Mayan octopuses behaved differently. They were more cautious and usually ignored the narrower hole instead of trying to fit. One possible reason is that they live in sandy, rocky areas and rarely need to squeeze through holes.

The team hopes the findings will inspire soft robots that can change shape to reach tight spaces. Current hole-fitting robots tend to be snake-shaped. Robyn Crook of San Francisco State University, who was not involved, suggested that slits or tubes may call for different strategies than round holes.

world.connect: Biology and engineering: a soft body that changes shape is a useful model for robots that must reach small, hard-to-reach places.

india.headline: Thousands Rally in Delhi Over a Voter-List Revision
india.deck: Opposition leaders want the chief election commissioner to resign; the Election Commission denies favouring any party.
body: A voter list is the register of who may vote, and in India it is checked and revised by the Election Commission. On Sunday 1 November, thousands of people rallied in New Delhi demanding that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi led the demonstration.
The argument is about numbers. The revision removed more than 130 million names from voter lists. Opposition parties say this hit Muslims and other minorities hardest.

The Election Commission answers that it does not favour any party, and says voters whose names were wrongly removed may register again. The BJP accuses opposition parties of undermining democracy, while Health Minister Jagat Prakash Nadda called the rally a 'carefully orchestrated drama'.
Al Jazeera described near-daily protests since late September. India's next general election is due in 2029.
india.why: A name on the voter list is what lets a family member vote. Relatives abroad who have Indian roots often follow how fairly the list is kept.
also: Delhi: Al Jazeera reported the capital's air turned hazardous days before Diwali, with residents reporting breathing difficulty and eye irritation.
Odisha: the state asked for Rs 2,526 crore in help after Cyclone Arnab and floods in Ganjam.

us.headline: Pay Rises 3.1% a Year, but Prices Are Rising Faster
us.deck: A strong jobs report did not end the squeeze on family budgets.
body: A family's budget depends on two numbers: what workers are paid and what things cost. Average hourly earnings in the US rose 3.1% over the past year, slightly more than the month before. Inflation, the rise in prices, reached 3.7% in September, so most workers are seeing real wage losses.
Fuel is a big reason. Gasoline was up about 34% from a year earlier.  Fuel prices are one reason living costs bite in both countries.
The hiring news was good. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. Analysts had expected 65,000 new jobs.

The Federal Reserve is watching. It raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point in September, the first rise in over three years, to a range of 3.75 to 4%, and held it in late October.  The next decision is set for 8 and 9 December.

us.headline: Pay Is Rising Slower Than Prices
body: Workers in the US now earn 3.1% more than a year ago. But prices rose 3.7% in September.
That means the same paycheck buys less. Gasoline is up about 34% over the year.
Still, employers added 165,000 jobs in October. The unemployment rate fell to 4.1%. That is the share of people looking for work who cannot find it, and it fell from 4.2% in September.
